html:
A short code of seventeen moral rules for officials of the Yamato court in Japan, dated to 604 and credited to Prince Shōtoku. It is known from the Nihon Shoki, a chronicle finished in 720.

It is not a constitution in the modern sense. It sets out how ministers should think and behave. The first article says that harmony is to be valued. Others tell officials to revere the three treasures of Buddhism, to obey the ruler's commands, to judge lawsuits fairly, to reward merit and to consult others on big matters.

The ideas come from Confucian and Buddhist thought, brought from China and Korea. The code marks the start of Japan's effort to build a centralised state on the Chinese model, which went on with the Taika Reform and the Taihō Code. Some scholars think it was written or polished later than 604.
sum: A short code of seventeen moral rules for officials of the Yamato court in Japan, dated to 604 and credited to Prince Shōtoku. It is known from the Nihon Shoki, a chronicle finished in 720.
